vignette: Thien is a 34-year-old chaplain of South Eastern Asian descent who has been struggling with the aftermath of a traumatic event—a mugging that occurred six months ago. At the time, he was walking through a crowded neighborhood on his way to conduct an evening service at a local community center. Thien remembers the smell of gasoline and exhaust from passing cars as well as the distinct sounds of heavy breathing from behind him. Suddenly, two men approached and demanded his wallet. The intensity and fear he experienced were overwhelming; the visual images of their faces and the crowding sensation in that narrow street remain vivid in his mind. In the days following the mugging, Thien found himself experiencing intense rage every time he thought about the event. He would often feel a surge of anger, recalling the sounds and smells from that night. The memory haunted him, especially when he encountered crowded places or heard heavy breathing sounds. These triggers evoked such strong reactions that he began to avoid similar situations altogether. Thien’s occupation as a chaplain means that his daily work involves interacting with people in various settings, often including crowded areas like community centers and hospitals. However, since the mugging, he has been increasingly reluctant to engage in these environments. He started cancelling appointments and found himself turning down invitations for community events. This avoidance led to strained relationships with colleagues who noticed his withdrawal and began questioning his commitment. The isolation exacerbated Thien’s negative beliefs about himself. He had come to believe that the event happened because of some inherent flaw or weakness, feeling a sense of character blame. Additionally, he was certain that he could not prevent such incidents from occurring again in the future, reinforcing feelings of helplessness. This belief was compounded by the thought that someone else would have known how to avoid or handle the situation differently. In his private moments, Thien grappled with intense guilt and shame for feeling unable to protect himself, which only deepened his negative self-assessment. He often found himself ruminating on what he could have done differently or how another person might have reacted more effectively in a similar situation. Despite these struggles, it was not until recently that Thien finally decided to seek help. The incident had begun to affect his ability to perform even the most basic aspects of his job. He became increasingly aware that avoiding crowded places and heavy breathing sounds only temporarily alleviated his anxiety but did nothing to address the underlying issues. What frightened him most was the fear that he might never feel safe again or that he would be unable to return to the full scope of his work as a chaplain. However, Thien also harbored hope that with help, he could regain a sense of control and peace. He hoped that therapy might provide tools for managing his reactions and enable him to reconnect with both his community and his professional life without feeling overwhelmed by the memories of that fateful night. Thien’s journey toward seeking help is marked by a deep desire to reclaim his identity and role as a chaplain, one that has been profoundly impacted by his traumatic experience. The weight of his negative beliefs and triggers remains significant, but he is determined to find a path forward where he can once again engage fully with his community and the people he serves.
